title: Nuclear family
description: Group of two parents and their children
wiki_lead:
A nuclear family – also called an elementary family, atomic family, or conjugal family – is a family group consisting of two parents and their children (one or more), typically living in one home residence. The term is used in contrast to both a single-parent family and a larger extended family (which may include grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins, and other blood relatives or community members). A nuclear family typically centers on a married couple that may have any number of children.
Definitions differ among observers. Some definitions restrict the term to only biological children who are full-blood siblings, others consider adopted or half- and step-siblings a part of the immediate family, but another definition allows for a step-parent and any mix of dependent children, including stepchildren and adopted children. 
Some sociologists and anthropologists consider the extended family structure to be the most common family structure in most cultures and at most times for humans, and the nuclear family to be a recent, modern departure.

A nuclear family – also called an elementary family, atomic family, or conjugal family – is a family group consisting of two parents and their children (one or more), typically living in one home residence. The term is used in contrast to both a single-parent family and a larger extended family (which may include grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins, and other blood relatives or community members). A nuclear family typically centers on a married couple that may have any number of children.
Definitions differ among observers. Some definitions restrict the term to only biological children who are full-blood siblings, others consider adopted or half- and step-siblings a part of the immediate family, but another definition allows for a step-parent and any mix of dependent children, including stepchildren and adopted children. 
Some sociologists and anthropologists consider the extended family structure to be the most common family structure in most cultures and at most times for humans, and the nuclear family to be a recent, modern departure.


Etymology
The term nuclear family first appeared in the United States in the early 20th century. The American dictionary Merriam-Webster dates the term back to 1924, and the British Oxford English Dictionary has a reference to the term from 1925; thus the term is relatively new. The phrase is taken from the general use of the noun nucleus, originating in the Latin nux, meaning 'nut', i.e. the core of something.

In its most common use, the term nuclear family refers to a household consisting of a mother, a father, and their children, all living in one household dwelling. George Murdock, an observer of families, offered an early description: The family is a social group characterized by common residence, economic cooperation and reproduction. It contains adults of both sexes, at least two of whom maintain a socially approved relationship, and one or more children, own or adopted, of the sexually cohabiting adults.
Many individuals are part of two nuclear families in their lives: the family of origin from which they are offspring, and the family of procreation for which they are a parent.
Alternative definitions have evolved to include family units with same-sex parents, adoption of members, and perhaps additional adult relatives who take on a cohabiting parental role.


History
DNA extracted from bones and teeth discovered at a 4,600-year-old Stone Age burial site in Germany has provided the earliest archaeological evidence of a family unit consisting of two parents with their multiple children.
Historians Alan Macfarlane and Peter Laslett, among other European researchers, say that nuclear families have been a primary arrangement in England since the 13th century. This primary arrangement was different from the typical arrangements in Southern Europe, in parts of Asia, and the Middle East, where it was common for young adults to remain residing in or marrying into a family home. Scholars such as Joseph Henrich have argued that this arrangement is a legacy of the Catholic Church’s medieval prohibition of cousin marriage, which dissolved extended kinship networks, thereby fostering the nuclear family structure. In England, multi-generational households were uncommon because young adults would save enough money to move out, into their own household once they married. Sociologist Brigitte Berger argued, "the young nuclear family had to be flexible and mobile as it searched for opportunity and property. Forced to rely on their own ingenuity, its members also needed to plan for the future and develop bourgeois habits of work and saving." Berger also mentions that this could be one of the reasons that the Industrial Revolution began in England and other Northwest European countries. However, the historicity of the nuclear family in England has been challenged by Cord Oestmann.

grok_lead: The nuclear family is a household unit comprising two parentsâtypically a married mother and father âand their dependent biological children, forming a self-contained domestic group independent of extended kin. This structure emphasizes direct parental investment in child-rearing, resource allocation, and socialization within the immediate unit, contrasting with extended families that incorporate grandparents, aunts, uncles, or other relatives under one roof or in close interdependence. Historically, nuclear families have predominated in Western Europe, including England, since at least the 13th century, challenging notions that they arose solely from industrialization or modernization; census and probate records show early prevalence of small, parent-child households amid broader kin networks. Empirical research links nuclear family stability to superior child outcomes, including lower rates of poor health (12% versus 22% in non-nuclear setups), enhanced academic performance, and reduced psychological risks, attributable to dual-parent involvement in supervision, emotional support, and economic provision. These advantages stem from causal mechanisms like consistent authority figures and undivided parental resources, though outcomes vary by factors such as parental conflict or socioeconomic status. In the United States, nuclear family prevalence peaked mid-20th century but has since declined sharply, with the share of adults living with a spouse and children falling from over 60% in 1970 to 37% by 2023, driven by rising divorce, nonmarital births, and delayed marriage. Fewer than half of children now reside in two-parent married households, correlating with elevated societal costs in welfare dependency, crime, and mental health burdens, though policy interventions like marriage promotion have shown mixed efficacy in reversing trends. Despite cultural shifts promoting diverse arrangements, longitudinal data affirm nuclear families' role in fostering intergenerational mobility and social trust when intact.
